Drain3 exists partly to solve this: it snapshots state to a file, Redis or Kafka and reloads on startup. Accuracy itself recovers quickly; identity does not.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Normalisation: one event, one shape (ECS and OCSF)
question: Why keep the raw text in event.original after normalising?
options: Schemas forbid deleting fields
ECS requires it for authentication events
It makes queries faster
It lets you re-parse old events after fixing a mapping bug and shows exactly what the source said
explain: Normalised fields are an interpretation. When an interpretation turns out wrong, the original is the only way to recover the truth for past events.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The detection lifecycle: hypothesis to retirement
question: Which ADS section would have warned the team that the MFA device rule gets noisy when a popular phone launches?
options: Goal
Priority
Categorization
False Positives
explain: Known benign triggers belong in False Positives, together with how to tell them apart. FireEye's 2020 detection (lesson 16) came from exactly such an alert, investigated despite that known noise.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Tuning and allowlisting without blinding yourself
question: Which allowlist is safest for a deployment agent that triggers the PowerShell rule?
options: CommandLine contains 'DeployAgent'
Exact ParentImage path under Program Files, plus the signer and the managed-host group
ParentImage endswith `\DeployAgent.exe`
Any event from user svc_deploy
explain: Only the exact-path option uses facts an attacker cannot cheaply forge: a path standard users cannot write to, a code-signing identity, and an inventory-defined scope. The others can be met by renaming a file, adding a word, or stealing one account.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Proving it works: purple teams, emulation and metrics
question: Incident detection times this quarter were 2, 4, 6, 8 and 700 hours. Which statement is accurate?
options: The median is 6 hours; the 700-hour incident should be examined on its own
The mean, 144 hours, describes a typical incident
The median is 144 hours
Both mean and median are 6 hours
explain: Mean = 720 / 5 = 144 hours, pulled up by one case; median = 6 hours. Report both and investigate the outlier.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
question: Ring Attention with 4 ranks and contiguous chunks shows rank 3 at full utilization and rank 0 mostly idle on a causal model. Which change fixes this without changing the math?
options: Increase the block size c
Assign each rank tokens or chunks spread across the sequence (striped or zigzag)
Switch to bidirectional attention
Reduce the number of KV heads
explain: The imbalance comes from the causal triangle: later query chunks attend to more keys. Striped Attention or Llama 3's chunk i plus chunk 2CP - 1 - i assignment gives every rank the same amount of unmasked work.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Recurrent depth at scale: prelude, core block and coda
question: Using the model card's rule (materialized params = 1.5r + 2 billion), what does running Huginn at r = 16 correspond to, and how many effective layers is that?
options: 26B and 68 layers
24B and 64 layers
26B and 64 layers
50B and 132 layers
explain: 1.5 x 16 + 2 = 26 billion. Effective depth is 2 prelude + 4 x 16 core + 2 coda = 68 layers. 50B and 132 layers is the r = 32 point.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
question: You change r from 8 to 16 but keep lora_alpha = 16. Compared with r = 8 and alpha = 16, what happens to the multiplier alpha/r?
options: It doubles from 1 to 2
It halves from 2 to 1
It stays 2, because PEFT rescales alpha automatically
It becomes alpha divided by the square root of r by default
explain: alpha/r goes from 16/8 = 2 to 16/16 = 1. With the default scaling the multiplier depends on r; only use_rslora=True switches to alpha/sqrt(r). Many recipes set alpha proportional to r (for example alpha = 2r) to keep the multiplier constant.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
question: A SISA system with S = 20 shards batches 60 uniformly random deletion requests before retraining. Roughly what fraction of the shard models must be retrained?
options: About 95%, almost every shard is hit at least once
About 5%, one shard per batch
About 33%, since 60 / 20 = 3 requests per shard on average
100% exactly, because 60 is larger than 20
explain: Each shard escapes all 60 requests with probability (1 - 1/20)^60, about 0.046, so about 95.4% of shards are hit at least once. It is not exactly 100% because some shards can get zero requests by chance. This saturation is why SISA's measured speed-ups shrink as requests pile up.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
question: A lab applies RMU to an open-weight model and publishes near-chance WMDP scores as evidence the model is safe to release. What is the strongest objection?
options: WMDP has too few questions to be meaningful
RMU always destroys general capabilities
With open weights anyone can fine-tune on related data, and RMU did not prevent relearning in the WMDP paper's own fine-tuning experiment
Near-chance scores prove the model was never trained on the data
explain: The WMDP appendix reports that fine-tuning an RMU-unlearned Mistral-7B on the forget corpus recovered performance, and Hu et al. show even benign related data can jog the knowledge back. RMU's stated threat model is a closed model unlearned just before serving, not a public release.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The PE format: headers, sections and what imports reveal
question: Where does Windows find the offset of the PE header in a file?
options: In the first two bytes, MZ
At the end of the file
In the .text section
In the 4-byte value at offset 0x3c of the MS-DOS stub
explain: Microsoft's specification: at location 0x3c the stub holds the file offset of the PE signature. In our file it was 0x80.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviours as indicators: persistence, credentials, ransomware
question: Which single event is the most urgent sign that ransomware encryption is imminent on a Windows host?
options: A new Run key value
A DNS query from a browser
A successful logon (event 4624)
vssadmin.exe deleting all shadow copies
explain: Deleting shadow copies removes a recovery option just before encryption (ATT&CK T1490). Run keys and logons happen in many benign situations; mass shadow deletion by a non-backup tool rarely does.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Sharing intelligence and writing the analysis report
question: You found an indicator in a customer's incident that could identify the customer. You want peer organisations to block it but not to learn the customer's identity. What is the best approach?
options: Post it publicly with TLP:CLEAR
Do not share anything
Share the technical indicator without identifying context, with a TLP label matching how far it may spread
Send the full report to everyone with TLP:RED
explain: Strip identifying context, keep the technical indicator, and label it (often TLP:AMBER or TLP:GREEN) so recipients know the limits. TLP:RED would stop it reaching most people who need it.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Shortlist then rerank: adaptive retrieval and funnel search
question: Single-shot exact search over 1,281,167 vectors at 2048 dims vs adaptive retrieval with D_s = 16, K = 200, D_r = 2048. Which term dominates the adaptive cost?
options: The rerank: 200 x 2048 = 409,600 multiply-adds
The shortlist scan: 16 x 1,281,167, about 20.5 million multiply-adds
Both are equal by design
Encoding the query, which grows with D_r
explain: The scan touches every vector: 20.5M multiply-adds. The rerank touches only 200 vectors: 0.41M. So the shortlist scan is about 98% of the 20.9M total, and speeding it up (smaller D_s, ANN, binary) gives the biggest win.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU
question: A Llama-style 70B model is trained with 8K-token sequences on 64 GPUs (8 per node). Which configuration fits the Megatron Core guidance best?
options: TP = 4, PP = 4, CP = 2, DP = 2
TP = 64, nothing else
TP = 1, PP = 64
TP = 16 across two nodes, DP = 4
explain: This is the guide's own example: TP stays inside a node, PP splits the 80 layers across nodes, CP = 2 handles the 8K sequence, and DP uses what is left (4 x 4 x 2 x 2 = 64). TP = 64 or 16 crosses nodes with all-reduces every layer; PP = 64 gives a huge bubble.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Why freed memory does not go back: pages, arenas, purging
question: In the 64-objects-per-page model, a workload frees 95% of its objects at random. What fraction of pages becomes returnable?
options: About 95%
About 3.8%
About 50%
Exactly 0%
explain: A page is empty only if all 64 objects died: 0.95^64 is about 0.0375, so about 3.8% of pages. The other 96% each hold at least one survivor and stay resident. Correlated lifetimes in real programs do better than this random model.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
question: A spin lock is implemented as `while LOCKED.swap(true, Acquire) {}` ... critical section ... `LOCKED.store(false, ORD)`. Which ORD is the weakest correct choice?
options: Relaxed
Acquire
SeqCst, because unlocking must be globally visible
Release
explain: The unlock must publish the critical section's writes to the next locker. That needs a Release store paired with the Acquire swap. Acquire is not even allowed on a plain store, Relaxed creates no happens-before, and SeqCst works but promises far more than needed.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
question: A developer removes the re-validation step: after `hp[me] = t; full_fence();` the code reads `t->next` directly. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, the fence already makes the hazard pointer visible
Another thread may have retired and freed t before the hazard pointer was published, so reading its next field touches freed memory
The CAS will always fail
The retired list will grow without bound
explain: Publishing only protects a node that is still in the structure at the moment the slot becomes visible. If t was unlinked and a scan ran between the load and the publish, the scan saw no slot and freed t. The re-read proves t was still reachable after the publish, so every later scan must see the slot.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
question: A Rust program uses crossbeam-epoch. Memory grows steadily, and a profiler shows one thread blocked on a channel receive inside a function that holds an `epoch::Guard`. What fixes it?
options: Increase the bag size from 64
Drop the guard (or call repin) before blocking on the channel
Switch the CAS to SeqCst (sequentially consistent) ordering
Call `pin()` more often on other threads
explain: The blocked thread stays pinned in an old epoch, so the global epoch cannot advance past it and every thread's garbage waits. Bag size and memory ordering do not change that. Holding guards only for short, non-blocking sections is the rule for any grace-period scheme.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Heap overflow: corrupting the neighbouring object
question: On Linux with glibc, a heap overflow often crashes later inside free() rather than at the bad write. What explains that?
options: free() is unsafe
The kernel delays signals
The overflow corrupted the allocator's size header of the next block, and free() trusts that header
glibc does not use headers
explain: glibc keeps a size header before each block. Overwriting it does not fault immediately; the allocator only notices, or misbehaves, when it later reads that corrupted size.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Uninitialized memory and type confusion
question: Why did build_reply print hunter2 although it never touched check_password's variable?
options: printf prints its previous output again when a buffer is empty
The compiler merged the two arrays on purpose
check_password returned the secret in a register that printf read
Both functions' frames used the same stack addresses, and returning from check_password left its bytes in place
explain: Frames are reused, not wiped. The uninitialized reply started with the bytes check_password left behind.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
question: A model trained on the Market-1501 training identities reaches high accuracy on held-out images of those same people. Why does that not tell you it will work for re-ID on Market-1501's test split?
options: Because the test images are smaller than training images
Because accuracy is not defined for embeddings
Because the test identities are different people, so what matters is whether distances generalize to unseen identities
Because re-ID only uses the gallery, never the query
explain: Re-ID test identities are disjoint from training identities. Closed-set accuracy on known people says little about whether the embedding separates new people. You need a retrieval evaluation on unseen identities.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
question: Your team wants to add k-reciprocal re-ranking to a live system that searches a gallery growing by millions of crops per day. What is the main concern?
options: It needs labeled data to retrain the model
It needs neighbor lists for gallery images too, so its cost grows with the gallery and must be recomputed as it changes
It only improves rank-1, never mAP
It only works with ArcFace features
explain: Re-ranking is unsupervised and needs no retraining, but it computes reciprocal neighbors from the gallery's own top-k lists. That is affordable on a fixed benchmark gallery and costly on a large, changing one.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
question: In a JMH run with forks set to 0, benchmark C is 30% slower when it runs after benchmark D than when it runs alone. What is the right fix?
options: Run each benchmark in its own forked JVM, as JMH does by default
Increase warm-up iterations so the JIT settles
Disable ASLR
Add a Blackhole to benchmark C
explain: C inherits JIT profiles from D in a shared JVM, the effect JMHSample_12_Forking demonstrates. More warm-up in the same JVM keeps the polluted profile. ASLR and Blackholes address layout noise and dead code, which are not the problem here.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
question: You serve a MoE with NVFP4 on B200s to speed up rollout but keep the trainer in BF16 to save engineering time. What do the Miles docs say?
options: Supported; add R3 to cover the drift
Supported only with --use-tis
Supported only on Hopper
Unsupported: NVFP4 rollout needs an NVFP4 trainer forward
explain: The compatibility table allows BF16 training with BF16, FP8 block-wise or MXFP8 rollout, but NVFP4 rollout pairs only with NVFP4 training. The report explains that NVFP4 requires every stage that touches the weights to quantize them.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady
question: LRB samples training examples uniformly over objects in the memory window rather than over requests. Why?
options: Sampling requests would be too slow to compute
Sampling requests over-represents popular objects, while the decisions LRB must learn are mostly about rarely requested objects it should evict
GBMs cannot train on duplicate objects
Objects that are never requested again would be sampled too often
explain: Per-request sampling picks a hot object once per request, so the dataset fills with objects that should obviously stay. The good evictions, objects beyond the boundary including those never requested again, would be rare. The paper samples over objects so both kinds are represented.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Low-rank joint compression: cache one latent, rebuild every head
question: In DeepSeek-V3, which tensors does an MLA layer write to the KV cache for each new token?
options: The per-head keys $k^C$ and values $v^C$
The query latent $c^Q$ and the key latent $c^{KV}$
The layer input $h_t$, since everything can be recomputed from it
The key-value latent $c^{KV}$ and the shared RoPE key $k^R$
explain: Only $c^{KV}$ (512) and $k^R$ (64) are cached. Queries are never cached. Caching $h_t$ (7168 wide) would be larger and would force recomputing projections for every past token.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, results
question: A blog says MLA alone cut DeepSeek-V2's KV cache by 93.3% vs MHA. What is wrong with that claim?
options: 93.3% is measured against DeepSeek 67B (a GQA model) for the deployed system, which also quantizes the cache; MLA vs MHA in matched models was 14% to 4% of the MHA cache
Nothing, that is exactly what the paper measured
MLA increases the KV cache
93.3% refers to training cost
explain: The abstract compares V2 to DeepSeek 67B. The matched MHA vs MLA comparison is Table 9: 15.6K vs 110.6K and 34.6K vs 860.2K elements per token.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Thousands of adapters: S-LoRA's unified paging and loading
question: A burst of requests touches 40 rarely used adapters at high rank. In S-LoRA's design, what is the most direct cost?
options: The base model must be reloaded
Requests for those adapters must wait for a merge
Adapter pages take space from the KV cache, reducing how many requests fit in a batch, and each adapter must be fetched from host memory
SGMV can no longer batch rows together
explain: Adapters live in host memory and are fetched on demand into the unified pool. Each active adapter uses pages that the KV cache could have used, so many large ones at once cut the batch size. Nothing is merged, and batching still works.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
question: In the toy, why does d2 (not relevant) outrank d7 (relevant) after fusing all four lists?
options: d2 has a higher cosine similarity
d2 appears in two lists while d7 appears in only one, and RRF sums contributions
RRF gives rank 1 a weight of zero
d7 was removed by deduplication
explain: RRF adds one term per list. d2 gets 1/62 + 1/65 = 0.03151; d7 gets only 1/61 = 0.01639 even though it was ranked first by q2. Agreement beats a single strong vote.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Candidate depth k and the recall ceiling
question: Your RAG search uses BM25 top 100 and a strong cross-encoder. You swap in a cross-encoder twice as large and nDCG@10 barely moves. Stage 1 recall@100 is 0.62. What is the most likely bottleneck?
options: The new cross-encoder is undertrained
The ceiling: 38% of relevant documents never reach the reranker, so stage 1 recall or k must improve
nDCG@10 cannot measure reranker quality
k = 100 is too deep and confuses the reranker
explain: With recall@100 of 0.62, the reranker never sees 38% of relevant documents. Bigger rerankers only reorder the 62% they receive. Raise the ceiling: hybrid first stage, better embeddings, or a larger k if the budget allows.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
question: A 10-token sequence is trained with n = 4 independent future heads. How many loss terms does it contribute (count head i as having 10 - i targets)?
options: 9, because only the next-token head counts
40, because each of 10 positions has 4 targets
36, because 4 x 9
explain: Head 1 has targets for positions 1 to 9, head 2 for positions 1 to 8, and so on: 9 + 8 + 7 + 6 = 30. Positions near the end have fewer valid future tokens, so the count is not simply 10 x 4.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
question: You serve a Gloeckle-style 4-token model with greedy decoding and enable self-speculative decoding with all 4 heads. What happens to the generated text?
options: It becomes more diverse because heads 2 to 4 inject their own choices
It is identical to greedy decoding with head 1; only the number of forward passes drops
It is identical only if every draft is accepted
It degrades slightly, which is the price of a 3x speedup
explain: Every emitted token is one that head 1 would have chosen given the same prefix: drafts are kept only when they match head 1's prediction, and the first mismatch is replaced by head 1's token. Acceptance rate changes speed, never content.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
question: You need to estimate SOAP's optimizer memory for a $4096 \times 4096$ matrix, counting state plus the gradient as the paper does. Which is closest?
options: 33.6M floats, one buffer like Muon
50.3M floats, the same as AdamW
117.4M floats
281 trillion floats, like full-matrix AdaGrad
explain: $2m^2 + 2n^2 + 3mn$ with $m = n = 4096$ is $33.6 + 33.6 + 50.3 \approx 117.4$ million. AdamW uses $3mn = 50.3$M (gradient, first and second moment); Muon uses about $2mn = 33.6$M (gradient and one momentum buffer).

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: The muP rules, layer by layer
question: Your model ties the input embedding and output unembedding weights. Which muP formulation from the paper fits best?
options: Table 3, because it is the main table
Neither; muP cannot be used with tied embeddings
Table 8, which gives input and output weights the same init and LR scaling and puts a 1/fan_in multiplier on the logits
SP with a smaller global learning rate
explain: Table 3 initializes output weights with variance $1/\text{fan\_in}^2$ but input weights with $1/\text{fan\_in}$, which conflicts if they are the same tensor. Table 8 is an equivalent formulation where all vector-like parameters share one rule and the width factor moves into a forward multiplier, so tying works. `MuSharedReadout` implements this.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin
question: In the cost model, sleeping costs C = 5 units and you spin for a budget B = 5 before sleeping. The lock turns out to be held for W = 3 units. What do you pay?
options: 5 units, because you always sleep eventually
10 units
8 units
3 units: the lock frees up during the spin
explain: W = 3 is within the budget, so you spin 3 units, take the lock, and never sleep. That equals the best in hindsight, min(3, 5) = 3.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
question: A table has 1 row that has been updated 3 times since it was inserted, and no VACUUM has run. How many tuples for that row are on disk?
explain: The insert created one tuple and each of the 3 updates wrote another, so there are 4 tuples. Only the newest has xmax = 0; the other 3 wait for VACUUM.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
question: An UPDATE changes only a non-indexed `last_seen` column, and the page has free space. What does HOT save compared with a normal update?
options: It avoids writing a new tuple version at all
It avoids new index entries, and lets old versions be pruned without VACUUM
It skips writing to the WAL
It makes the update visible to concurrent snapshots
explain: HOT still writes a new tuple version (MVCC requires it), but on the same page and without new index entries. Intermediate versions can be pruned during normal page access.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Scoring whole sequences: transitions and Viterbi by hand
question: Your BIO tagger has no CRF and sometimes emits `O I-ORG I-ORG`. Which response still leaves that sequence possible?
options: Add a CRF layer so the training loss sees label transitions and Viterbi cannot take an invalid one
Switch to BIOES so the output layer has 17 labels instead of 9
Keep the independent softmax but mask out transitions the scheme forbids during decoding
Decode with a beam that only extends well-formed BIO prefixes
explain: BIOES makes the tag set larger and the end of a span explicit, but with independent per-token softmaxes nothing rules out an impossible sequence: you can still emit O then I-ORG, now with 17 labels. The other three all make the invalid path unreachable, either in the loss or in the decoder.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
question: With NSA's settings ($d=16$, $n=16$, $l'=64$, $w=512$), which term of the per-query key count dominates at a 1M-token context?
options: The compressed tokens, about $t/d \approx 65{,}500$
The selected tokens, $nl' = 1024$
The window, $w = 512$
All three are equal
explain: Selection and window are fixed sizes. Compression grows linearly with $t$ at rate $1/d$, so at long context it dominates: about 65,534 of roughly 67,070 keys at 1,048,576 tokens.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
question: Why does aHash squash the image to 8x8 without keeping the aspect ratio?
options: So that the hash fits in a 64-bit integer, which is the only reason
Because grayscale conversion only works on square images
To keep high-frequency detail that distinguishes near copies
So that a resized or stretched copy reduces to nearly the same 64 pixels and therefore the same bits
explain: The shrink is what makes the hash scale-invariant: every size and aspect ratio of the same picture is crushed to the same 8x8 grid. It also discards high frequencies on purpose, the opposite of the last option.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
question: Why does PDQ use 256 bits where pHash uses 64?
options: 256-bit integers are faster to XOR
More bits keep unrelated images far apart even in web-scale collections, where a 64-bit hash with a useful threshold yields many chance matches
The DCT requires 256 outputs
To store the image's color histogram
explain: With 64 bits and threshold 10, uniform random hashes already give about 10 chance candidates per query in a billion images. With 256 bits and threshold 31, the random-collision rate is astronomically small; the PDQ authors call 256 bits appropriate for web scale.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Colocated vs non-colocated generation, and how weights are refit
question: A single node has 8 GPUs. You set colocated.enabled: false and colocated.resources.gpus_per_node: 8. What happens?
options: Training and generation each get 8 GPUs
Setup fails because training would get 8 - 8 = 0 GPUs
NeMo RL falls back to colocated mode
Generation gets 4 and training gets 4
explain: On one node, training gets cluster.gpus_per_node minus the inference GPUs. The setup asserts that the result is greater than 0, so this config is rejected.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: VLANs, VLAN hopping and 802.1X port authentication
question: A trunk's native VLAN is 1 and the guest Wi-Fi bridge is also on VLAN 1. Which change best removes the double-tagging risk?
options: Add more VLANs
Turn on DHCP snooping
Give the trunk a native VLAN that no user or guest port uses
Move the payment terminals to VLAN 2
explain: Double tagging needs the sender to be on the trunk's native VLAN, because that is the tag the first switch strips. Making the native VLAN one with no user ports removes the precondition. The other options do not touch the tag handling.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: BGP hijacks and route leaks: the MyEtherWallet case
question: An AS announces 205.251.192.0/24 while the owner announces 205.251.192.0/23. Where accepted, which wins, and why?
options: The /23, because it was announced first
Whichever has the shorter AS path
The /24, because routers choose the longest (most specific) matching prefix
Neither: routers drop overlapping prefixes
explain: Longest prefix match is applied before any BGP preference between routes: a /24 is more specific than a /23, so destinations inside it follow the /24. AS path length only decides between announcements of the same prefix.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: DDoS: three classes, and the maths of amplification
question: Why did GitHub's monitoring watch the ratio of ingress to egress traffic rather than just ingress?
options: Egress is cheaper to measure
Akamai required it
Ingress is encrypted
A web service normally sends far more than it receives, so a sudden inversion is a strong DDoS signal that ordinary traffic growth does not cause
explain: Serving pages and git data means egress normally exceeds ingress. Floods only add ingress, so the ratio flips. A legitimate traffic spike raises both directions together and leaves the ratio roughly stable.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Segmentation, zero trust and the Target breach
question: Which statement matches NIST SP 800-207's idea of zero trust?
options: Devices inside the corporate network are trusted; outside ones are not
Once a user logs in to the VPN, they may access any internal system
Zero trust means blocking all traffic
Every access request is authenticated and authorised per session, using policy that includes device state, regardless of where on the network it comes from
explain: Zero trust removes implicit trust from network location. The log-in-to-the-VPN model is exactly the implicit trust zone it replaces. It does not mean blocking everything, but deciding each session explicitly.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Ethernet frames and MAC addresses
question: You capture traffic on your laptop, plugged into a switched office LAN, in promiscuous mode (the card hands every frame it receives to the capture program, not only frames addressed to it). What will you see by default?
options: Every frame sent by every device on the LAN
Only frames to or from your laptop, plus broadcast and multicast frames
Nothing at all, because switches encrypt frames
Only frames whose source MAC matches your OUI
explain: Promiscuous mode makes your card accept every frame it receives, but the switch only sends your port the frames meant for you plus broadcasts and multicasts. Seeing other hosts' traffic needs a hub, a mirror port on the switch (a port configured to receive copies of other ports' traffic), or tricking the switch or the hosts, which is exactly what layer 2 attacks try.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: TCP: handshake, sequence numbers, flags and teardown
question: The client's ISN is 7000. It sends SYN, completes the handshake, then sends 250 bytes. What acknowledgment number should the server send after receiving them?
explain: The SYN consumes sequence number 7000, so data starts at 7001. 250 bytes cover 7001 to 7250, and the acknowledgment names the next expected byte: 7251.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTPS and TLS at a glance: what encryption hides and what it does not
question: A user connects to `https://bank.example`. Why can a device in the middle (say, after ARP spoofing) not simply read the traffic by pretending to be the bank?
options: Because ARP spoofing does not work on Wi-Fi
Because the device cannot present a certificate for bank.example signed by an authority the browser trusts, so the handshake fails or warns
Because TLS hides the IP addresses
Because port 443 cannot be intercepted
explain: The device can relay packets, but to decrypt it must complete the TLS handshake as bank.example, and that requires a trusted certificate and the matching private key. Without them the browser shows an error. The attack then depends on the user ignoring the warning.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
question: A service is started with `numactl --membind=0` on a 2-node box. Node 0 has 64 GiB, node 1 has 64 GiB, and the service grows to 80 GiB. What happens?
options: The extra 16 GiB is allocated on node 1 automatically
The kernel switches the process to interleave mode
Allocations that node 0 cannot satisfy fail, because bind never falls back to node 1
explain: MPOL_BIND restricts allocation to the listed nodes. numactl(8) says allocation will fail when there is not enough memory on them. If spilling to node 1 is acceptable, use --preferred=0 instead.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Why flash cannot overwrite a page in place
question: A drive uses a direct-mapped layout with 256 KB erase blocks of 4 KB pages. The host overwrites a single 4 KB page. How many page programs does the flash perform?
options: 1, because only one page changed
63, the other live pages
64, the whole block is rewritten after the erase
128, one read and one program per page
explain: After erasing, every page of the block is blank, so all 64 pages (63 preserved plus the new one) must be programmed. That is 64x more flash writing than the host asked for, and the block takes one more P/E cycle per host write.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
question: A host driver reaps completions by checking the phase tag. After the CQ wraps from the last slot back to slot 0, what must the driver do?
options: Nothing: new entries always have phase tag 1
Reset every phase tag in the queue to 0
Read the controller's CQ tail register
Flip the phase value it expects, because the controller now writes the opposite bit
explain: On each wrap the controller inverts the phase tag it writes. The host tracks the expected value and flips it when its head wraps. The CQ tail is internal to the controller and not visible to the host.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Training and tuning a detector in practice
question: You call `model.predict(img, conf=0.25, iou=0.7)` and see two boxes on one car with IoU 0.6 between them. Which change removes the duplicate?
options: Set iou=0.5 so NMS suppresses boxes overlapping by more than 0.5
Raise conf to 0.5
Set iou=0.9
Set max_det=1
explain: Here `iou` is the NMS threshold: boxes overlapping a higher-scoring box by more than it are removed. At 0.7 a 0.6 overlap survives; at 0.5 it is suppressed. Raising conf might drop the duplicate only if its score is low, and max_det=1 would discard every other car too.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Keeping object storage off the hot read path
question: In Neon, why does a COMMIT not include the latency of an object storage PUT?
options: Postgres batches commits for up to a second
Durability comes from a majority of safekeepers storing the WAL; pages reach object storage later, off the commit path
The compute node's local NVMe is replicated
Object storage writes are done with S3 Express One Zone
explain: Neon defines commit as WAL acknowledged by a quorum of safekeepers. The pageserver materializes pages and uploads them to object storage asynchronously. If a safekeeper dies, the quorum continues; if the pageserver dies, its state is rebuilt from WAL and object storage.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Traces: spans, context propagation, and what sampling throws away
question: Which setup guarantees a complete trace for every request that returned a 500?
options: Tail sampling in the collector, which buffers a trace's spans and decides once they are complete
Head sampling at 1 in 10 plus a longer retention period
A trace-id ratio sampler at 0.01, since its decision is deterministic
Setting the sampled bit at the gateway only when the gateway sees an error
explain: Only a decision made after the spans exist can condition on the error. Longer retention keeps dropped spans dropped. A deterministic ratio sampler is still a ratio. The last option fails because the gateway must inject traceparent before the request runs, so at decision time the error has not happened yet, and the downstream spans would already have been dropped.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Scoring OCR output: edit distance, CER and WER
question: You must pick one metric to decide whether an invoice-total extractor is good enough for automatic payment. Which is most appropriate?
options: Average CER over all page text
Average WER over all page text
Exact match of the normalized total field per document
Detection F-score of text boxes
explain: Payment needs the exact amount. Page-level CER can look excellent while the one field that matters has a wrong digit. Field-level exact match after agreed normalization measures what the business cares about.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Discretionary vs mandatory access control, and the LSM hooks
question: Ana runs `chmod 777 /home/ana/notes.txt`. The SELinux policy does not allow the web server's domain to read files in home directories. Can a compromised web server read the file?
options: Yes, because 777 lets everyone read
Yes, because DAC is checked last and wins
No, because the MAC check runs after DAC and refuses
No, because chmod 777 removes read permission
explain: Both checks must say yes. DAC passes (others have r), then the LSM hook asks the mandatory policy, which the file's owner cannot override, and it refuses.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Dropping privileges correctly, and sudo's Baron Samedit
question: Why must setresgid come before setresuid when dropping from root?
options: After the UIDs leave 0 the process loses the capability needed to change GIDs, so a later setresgid would fail and leave root's group in place
Group IDs are checked first by the kernel
setresuid resets the groups automatically
It does not matter
explain: Changing GIDs and supplementary groups needs CAP_SETGID. Dropping the UIDs first clears the capabilities, so the group change fails, and if the return value is not checked the process keeps group 0.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: chroot is not a boundary, and Leaky Vessels shows why
question: Which of runc 1.1.12's fixes also protects against file descriptor leaks nobody has found yet?
options: Closing all internal descriptors before execve and checking that the working directory is inside the container
Marking the one known cgroup descriptor O_CLOEXEC
Renaming /sys/fs/cgroup
Disabling WORKDIR in Dockerfiles
explain: Fixing the known leak removes one hole. Closing every non-stdio descriptor and verifying the working directory with getcwd stop the whole class, which is why the advisory recommends them to other runtimes.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: What goes wrong: the confused deputy and TOCTOU races
question: Which change removes the TOCTOU window in a setuid program that calls access() then open()?
options: Dropping the separate check and opening the file with the caller's own effective UID (and O_NOFOLLOW)
Calling access() twice
Adding sleep() between the calls
Checking that the path string does not contain /etc
explain: Any separate check leaves a gap. Making the open itself run with the caller's identity lets the kernel do the check atomically on the file actually opened.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CMake in three phases: configure, generate, build
question: A crash only happens in your Release build, and you need a debugger with line numbers but the same optimization level class. Which build type is the best first try?
options: Debug, since it has -g
RelWithDebInfo, which keeps optimization (-O2 for GCC) and adds -g
MinSizeRel, since it keeps NDEBUG
An empty CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE
explain: Debug drops optimization (only -g) and keeps asserts on, which can hide an optimizer-dependent or NDEBUG-dependent bug. RelWithDebInfo is optimized, defines NDEBUG like Release, and keeps debug info. It is still -O2 rather than Release's -O3, so the bug may move, but it is the closest standard type.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Jobs, needs and matrices: how one push becomes many runs
question: A matrix has `os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]`, `python: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]` and one `exclude` entry for `os: windows-latest, python: "3.10"`. How many jobs does the matrix create?
explain: Product $2 \times 4 = 8$, minus the one excluded combination gives 7. Each is a separate job on a separate runner.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
question: A PR fixes a real bug and adds a test, but the reviewer would have named one helper function differently and prefers a slightly different loop style that the style guide does not mention. Under Google's standard, what should the reviewer do?
options: Request changes until both points are fixed, since the PR is not yet perfect
Approve, optionally leaving the naming and loop points as Nit: comments
Close the PR and write the fix themselves in their preferred style
Approve only after a third reviewer agrees on the naming
explain: The change definitely improves code health (a fixed bug plus a test). Style points not in the style guide are personal preference, so they should not block. Marking them Nit: keeps the feedback without delaying the merge.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Why reviewer response time dominates time to merge
question: Using the model with n = 2 and F = 2, a reviewer who used to take 8 hours per response now takes 4. How much does total time to merge drop?
options: From 28 h to 24 h
From 28 h to 16 h
From 28 h to 14 h
It does not change, since the author's work is the same
explain: Total is (n+1)R + nF. Before: 3 x 8 + 4 = 28 h. After: 3 x 4 + 4 = 16 h. Each hour saved per response is saved on all three rounds, so 4 hours faster per response saves 12 hours in total.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
question: Why does QEMU decline AI-generated patches even when the contributor fully understands and tests them?
options: Because AI code is always lower quality
Because the contributor cannot confidently certify the DCO when the copyright and license status of AI output is unsettled
Because it cannot be reviewed on a mailing list
Because QEMU forbids all tools, including static analysis
explain: QEMU's concern is provenance: the Signed-off-by line certifies the DCO, and with unclear licensing of AI output the project will not take the legal risk. It explicitly allows AI use for research, debugging and static analysis whose output is not in the patch.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
question: You rebase, your IDE silently runs `git fetch` every few minutes, and a maintainer pushed to your PR branch an hour ago. You run `git push --force-with-lease`. What happens?
options: It is rejected with stale info, because the maintainer's commit is newer than your rebase
It succeeds and overwrites the maintainer's commit, because the background fetch already updated your remote-tracking ref
It succeeds and keeps both, because a lease merges the histories
It is rejected because leases cannot be used on forks
explain: A bare lease compares the remote with your remote-tracking ref. The background fetch moved that ref to the maintainer's commit, so the lease matches and the forced update goes through. `--force-if-includes` would catch this, because the commit never appeared in your branch's reflog.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: License compatibility: can these two pieces of code be combined?
question: You want to copy an Apache-2.0 function into a Linux kernel driver (GPL-2.0-only). Which is correct?
options: Allowed, Apache-2.0 is permissive so it fits any project
Allowed, if you keep the NOTICE file
Not allowed as is: the FSF does not consider Apache-2.0 compatible with GPLv2
Allowed, because the kernel has a syscall exception
explain: Apache-2.0 is compatible with GPLv3 only. Its patent termination and indemnification terms are restrictions GPLv2 does not permit, so a GPL-2.0-only work cannot absorb it. The syscall exception concerns user programs calling the kernel, not code inside it.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Noise and bias: making before and after comparable
question: After `pyperf system tune` and CPU pinning, your runs vary by only 0.1%, and the patched build is 1.5% faster in every run. What can you still not conclude?
options: That the result is affected by noise
That the 1.5% comes from your change rather than a layout or order effect that favors the patched build
That the benchmark ran at all
That pyperf was installed correctly
explain: Low noise makes the gap statistically clear, but it says nothing about bias. Run order, code layout or environment size can shift one build consistently. Interleaving, rebuilding with different layouts or another machine tests for that.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Trace one request: a Redis GET from socket to reply
question: In a plugin-based web framework, `git grep -n -w handle_upload` finds only the definition and one line `routes = {"/upload": handle_upload}`. What is the best next search to find who runs it?
options: Conclude the function is dead code and propose deleting it
Search for `handle_upload(` with -w until a call appears
Search for where `routes` is read, for example `git grep -n -w routes`, to find the dispatcher that calls through the table
Search the tests for handle_upload
explain: A name stored in a table with no direct call is dynamic dispatch, as with Redis's command table. The caller looks up the table and calls the stored function, so search for the table's readers. Tests can help confirm behavior, but they do not show the production caller.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
question: Which repro is most likely to get a fast response on a library's issue tracker?
options: A link to a 2 GB dataset plus the 40-line script that loads it
A 3-row DataFrame built inline, the 6 lines that fail, and the full traceback
A screenshot of a notebook cell and its error output
Your entire notebook exported as a file
explain: Inline, artificial data plus a few failing lines and the full text traceback is copy-paste runnable. Downloads, screenshots and whole notebooks all push work onto the maintainer.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
question: Your PR moves `parser.c` into `lib/` and, while there, fixes an off-by-one in the moved function. What does the kernel guide recommend?
options: Keep both in one patch so the history shows the fix where the code now lives
Fix the bug first, then move the code in a second patch, or move first and fix second, but never modify code in the patch that moves it
Move the code and reformat it in the same patch, but put the fix separately
Leave the move out entirely; moves are never accepted
explain: The guide says not to modify moved code at all in the patch that moves it. That keeps the move verifiable as a pure move, and the fix shows up as a small, readable diff that history tools can track.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
question: Why does vLLM avoid a block size of 1 even though it minimizes wasted slots?
options: Block tables cannot store more than 1024 entries
Copy-on-write needs at least two tokens per block
Prefix caching only works with block sizes that are powers of two
The kernel processes fewer positions in parallel per fetch, underusing the GPU
explain: The paper explains that more tokens per block let the PagedAttention kernel process more positions in parallel. Too small underuses the GPU, too large raises internal fragmentation and lowers sharing. 16 was the default it chose.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Authorisation: scope, rules of engagement and permission
question: Why does the scope guard check the exclude list before the in-scope ranges?
options: It is faster
Python requires it
Excluded systems usually sit inside the in-scope ranges, so checking inclusion first would wrongly allow them
The order does not matter
explain: An exclude list is almost always a carve-out from a larger allowed range. If inclusion were checked first and returned early, the payment systems at .70 would be scanned.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: certificate logs, search engines and leaked code
question: A developer pushed an AWS key to a public repository, noticed an hour later, and pushed a commit deleting it. What should happen now?
options: Nothing more; the key is gone
Make the repository private and keep the key
Rewrite history first, then decide about the key next week
Revoke and rotate the key immediately and check its usage logs, because it remains in Git history and may already have been copied
explain: Deleting in a new commit leaves the old commit intact, and public repositories are scanned constantly. GitHub's guidance is to rotate immediately; history rewriting is secondary.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Web enumeration: crawling, content discovery and fingerprinting
question: A site's robots.txt contains `Disallow: /internal-reports/`. Is that a security control?
options: No: robots.txt is a public request to well-behaved crawlers, and it advertises the path to anyone who reads it
Yes: browsers refuse to open disallowed paths
Yes: search engines must legally obey it
Only if the file is encrypted
explain: WSTG says robots.txt should not be considered a mechanism to enforce restrictions. Sensitive paths need authentication, not a polite note.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Attack surface management: recon as a defender
question: Why did organisations with a working attack surface inventory respond faster to MOVEit in 2023?
options: They could see within minutes whether they ran an internet-facing MOVEit server and block or patch it, instead of first discovering what they owned
They were immune to SQL injection
Inventory tools patch software automatically
Attackers avoided them
explain: Exploitation began before disclosure. The deciding factor in the first hours was knowing your exposure, which is what ASM provides.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
question: A thread profile shows `hash_lookup` as a 5% tower under `parse` and a 25% tower under `index`, and nowhere else. What share of samples include hash_lookup?
options: 25%, take the widest tower
15%, the average
You cannot tell without the call count
explain: The same function under different callers appears as separate towers. Since no stack can contain both (they are disjoint paths here), the shares add: 5% + 25% = 30%, which is what the search feature reports.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Flushes, fences and the order things become durable
question: A record has two 8-byte fields, version and value, in different cache lines, and you update both in place with two ordinary stores, then persist both. A crash happens before the persist completes. How many of the 4 combinations of old and new fields can appear after reboot?
options: Only 2: all old or all new
3: the hardware never persists value before version
1: the persist call makes the update atomic
4, two of which are torn mixes of old and new
explain: Each 8-byte field is failure-atomic on its own, but together they are 16 bytes: old/old, new/new, old/new and new/old are all reachable, so 2 of the 4 are torn. pmem_persist is explicitly not atomic. You need an out-of-place copy or a log.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: The persuasion levers every lure pulls
question: Which pair best matches Stajano and Wilson's 'time' principle and Cialdini's 'authority' principle in a phishing email?
options: 'Your mailbox is 98 percent full' and 'Click to view your photo'
'Thanks for your order' and 'Your colleagues liked this post'
'Unsubscribe here' and 'Sent from my iPhone'
'Reply within 1 hour or your account is closed' and 'Message from the Head of Security'
explain: The deadline is time pressure, which pushes fast and shallow decisions. A sender styled as a head of security borrows authority. The other pairs mix weaker cues (curiosity, reciprocity, social proof) or none.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: SPF: which servers may send for a domain
question: corp.example's record is 'v=spf1 include:a.example include:b.example ... -all' with 11 include terms, each listing only ip4 ranges. Mail arrives from a server listed only in the 11th include. What happens?
options: SPF passes for everyone
Evaluation exceeds the DNS lookup limit and returns permerror
Only the first 10 includes are used
Receivers merge the extra include into the next record
explain: RFC 7208 caps DNS-querying terms at 10 during one evaluation. Reaching the 11th include exceeds the cap, so the result must be permerror, which is not a pass: this legitimate server gets no SPF credit. Servers matched earlier still pass.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Reading headers to triage a suspicious message
question: Which header detail is the hardest for an external sender to fake?
options: The display name in From
The IP address in the Received header written by your own border server
The bottom Received header's IP address
The Message-ID
explain: Your own server wrote that line using the address of the TCP connection it actually accepted. All the other fields, including lower Received lines, are text the sender (or a relay) controlled. Behind proxies or relays, it is the last hop rather than the true origin, but it is a fact, not a claim.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Business email compromise and invoice fraud
question: A real supplier's mailbox was compromised. The fraudulent 'new bank details' email passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC for the supplier's domain. What control would most reliably have stopped the payment?
options: Moving your own domain to p=reject
Scanning the email's attachments in a sandbox
A rule that bank detail changes are confirmed by calling the supplier on a number already on file
Blocking all emails that mention 'bank'
explain: The email is authentic in every technical sense, so authentication and filtering cannot help. Your own DMARC protects your domain, not the supplier's. A call-back on a known number reaches the real supplier, who did not send the request.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
question: `struct S { char a; double d; char b; };` on x86-64. What are `offsetof(S, d)` and `sizeof(S)`?
options: 1 and 10
8 and 17
4 and 16
8 and 24
explain: a at 0, then padding to 8 for d (alignment 8), d fills 8 to 15, b at 16, end at 17, rounded up to a multiple of 8 gives 24.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
question: A gym camera sees a tight group of three people, and the person detector returns only two boxes because NMS suppressed one overlapping box. What does a top-down pose system output?
options: Three skeletons, because the keypoint network sees all joints in the crop
Two skeletons; the suppressed person gets no pose at all
Three skeletons, but the third has low scores
Zero skeletons, because the boxes overlap
explain: The keypoint network only runs on boxes the detector returned. A person lost at the detection stage is lost for good: this is the early commitment problem of top-down methods.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
question: A pgvector query uses HNSW with ef_search = 40, WHERE tenant_id = 7 (0.5% of rows) and LIMIT 10. It usually returns 0 rows. What is the cause?
options: The HNSW graph is corrupted and needs a REINDEX
The filter runs after a 40-candidate scan; with s = 0.005 the expected survivors are 0.2, and P(zero) = 0.995^40 is about 82%
LIMIT 10 is applied before the WHERE clause, so the planner discards matches
HNSW cannot index tables that contain a tenant_id column
explain: Post-filtering on 40 candidates gives 40 x 0.005 = 0.2 expected matches, and the probability of none is 0.995^40 = 0.82. The index is fine; the filter just sees too few candidates. Iterative scans, a partial index, or a B-tree driven exact scan fix it (lesson 4).

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
question: Which workload is most likely latency-bound once its data is far larger than the caches?
options: Summing a large float array
Copying a 2 GB buffer with memcpy
Descending a pointer-based binary search tree with random keys
Adding two large vectors element by element
explain: Each tree level's child pointer comes from the node just loaded, so misses happen one after another. The other three compute every address from a loop index, so many lines can be requested in parallel and the limit is bytes per second.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Bandwidth-bound code: count the bytes, skip the reads
question: A single-threaded loop streams through a 4 GB array and achieves 11 GB/s on a server whose memory system delivers 150 GB/s across all cores. Adding software prefetches does not help. What is the most promising next step?
options: Switch to non-temporal stores, since it must be bandwidth-bound
Convert the array to a linked list
Split the work across several threads so more lines are in flight in total
Disable the hardware prefetcher
explain: 11 of 150 GB/s is far from peak, so this is not the bandwidth wall. A single core's concurrency (fill buffers plus L2 queues) caps it, as Little's law predicts. More cores bring more miss slots. Non-temporal stores reduce bytes, which matters only near the peak.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 3: setuid, capabilities, kernel bugs, docker group
question: Your patch tool reports that the fixed kernel for Dirty Pipe was installed yesterday. `uname -r` shows the old version. What is the state of the host?
options: Protected: the package is installed
Protected only for new processes
Still vulnerable: the old kernel is the one running until a reboot or live patch
Partly protected: half the kernel is updated
explain: The kernel in memory is the one that booted. Installing a new kernel package changes files in /boot, not the running code. Until the host reboots into it, or a live patch is applied, the bug is still there.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Credentials are the real currency: where they live on a host
question: CISA found NotPetya also infected fully patched Windows machines. What made that possible?
options: Credentials stolen from memory were reused with built-in admin tools (WMIC, PsExec)
EternalBlue worked on patched systems too
It exploited a zero-day in Windows Update
Patched machines had SMBv1 re-enabled
explain: EternalBlue only worked against unpatched SMBv1. The modified Mimikatz plus WMIC or PsExec route needed no vulnerability, just valid credentials, so patching did nothing to stop it.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Defending the path: segmentation, admin hygiene, EDR, HSE timeline
question: PwC found several detections in the HSE network weeks before the ransomware ran. What was the main failure?
options: There were no security tools at all
The attacker used an unknown zero-day exploit
Logs were encrypted by the ransomware before anyone could see them
Detections did not lead to an investigation and response in time
explain: Antivirus saw Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz on 31 March, hospitals saw alerts in May, and a provider flagged unhandled threats the day before. None became an incident investigation in time. Where the Department of Health did act, the ransomware was largely prevented.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Using a PRM: reranking, step-level search and RL
question: In process-supervised GRPO, two outputs have identical first steps with the same PRM reward. Why can their first-step tokens get opposite-sign advantages?
options: Normalization uses a different mean per output
The KL penalty differs between the outputs
Each token's advantage sums the normalized rewards of its own step and all later steps, so later steps differ
Only the last step's reward matters
explain: The advantage for a token is the sum of normalized step rewards at or after its step. In the example both first steps normalize to 0.77, but output 2's later step (-1.92) makes its first-step advantage -1.15.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a context switch, step by step
question: A thread calls `pthread_mutex_lock` on a lock another thread holds, and it sleeps until the lock is free. How is this counted?
options: As an involuntary switch, because the thread did not want to stop
As a voluntary switch, because it gave up the CPU before its slice ended to wait for a resource
It is not a context switch, because the lock is in user space
As a system call but not a switch
explain: Blocking on anything (I/O, a futex-based lock, sleep) is a voluntary switch in the getrusage sense: the thread released the CPU early. Involuntary means it was preempted while it still wanted to run.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Training per-slice codebooks and encoding a vector
question: A colleague trains one PQ codebook per sub-vector but forgets to use the same dimension split at encoding time (they split the database vectors in a different order). What happens?
options: Nothing, because k-means is permutation invariant
Codes are still valid but 2x larger
Every sub-vector is matched against a codebook learned on different dimensions, so reconstructions and distances are garbage
Only the first sub-vector is affected
explain: Codebook C_j only knows the distribution of slice j. Feeding it a different slice produces arbitrary nearest-centroid choices. The split (and any rotation applied before it) is part of the model and must be identical for training, encoding and querying.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: APE and OPRO: language models that write prompts
question: Which piece of information does OPRO's optimizer see that APE's proposal step does not?
options: The target model's log probabilities
A sorted list of earlier instructions with their measured scores
The test set labels
Gradients of the loss with respect to the prompt tokens
explain: OPRO's meta-prompt carries the optimization trajectory: past instructions and their training accuracies in ascending order. APE proposes from demonstrations, and its resampling only paraphrases a kept instruction. Neither method looks at test labels or gradients.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Managed prompt optimizers and a practical workflow
question: Bedrock's Advanced Prompt Optimization reads your Lambda metric's source code and docstrings. What is the practical consequence?
options: Metric code is ignored if you also give ground truth
A vague or buggy metric steers the rewriting toward the wrong goal, so make the metric precise and test it before the job
You must write the metric in natural language only
The judge model will be fine-tuned on your docstrings
explain: The docs say both the dataset and the metric shape optimization quality, and that the evaluation steers the rewriting. Like every optimizer in this course, it maximizes what you measure, not what you meant.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: The funnel: from 100 backbones to a binder that works
question: Your generator produces 100 backbones and 8 sequences each, and 0 backbones pass the 2 Angstrom filter. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Raise the scRMSD threshold to 5 Angstrom so some designs pass
Fix the backbone generator: a correlated-failure pattern across all 8 sequences points at the geometry, not the sequence design
Sample 100 sequences per backbone instead of 8
Switch AF2 from single-sequence to full MSA mode so predictions improve
explain: Sequences for one backbone are strongly correlated, so a uniform failure across all 8 is evidence about the backbones. The measured jump from 28 percent at M = 8 to only 40 percent at M = 100 shows how little extra sampling buys. Relaxing the threshold or giving AF2 an MSA hides the problem rather than fixing it.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Regular expressions: counting failed logins per address
question: Which log shape most strongly suggests credential stuffing rather than password guessing?
options: One address, one username, 300 failures
Many addresses, each failing once on the root account over a month
A single failed login at 3 a.m.
One address, 40 different usernames, one attempt each, then a success
explain: Stuffing replays known pairs: each account is tried about once, with whatever password leaked for it, and some succeed because of password reuse. Many attempts on one account is guessing. The success at the end is the urgent part: it means a working stolen credential.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Enriching indicators: threat-intel lookups within rate limits
question: Your free-tier key allows 4 lookups per minute. A morning alert lists 600 unique hashes. With 15-second pacing and no 429s, roughly how long does enrichment take?
options: About 2.5 minutes
About 40 minutes
About 2.5 hours, and the free daily allowance of 500 runs out first anyway
About 15 seconds, because the requests run in parallel
explain: 600 lookups at 4 per minute is 150 minutes. The Public API also caps a key at 500 requests per day, so the last 100 would fail. This is the arithmetic that justifies a licensed feed, a local cache shared across runs, or deduplicating and prioritizing before you look anything up.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym expansion on the toy corpus: recall up, precision at risk
question: In the toy corpus, why did vehicle contribute 0.896 to d3 while car contributed only 0.666 to d1, both in 4-token documents?
options: vehicle appears in 1 document and car in 2, so vehicle has the higher IDF
Synonyms get an automatic 1.35x boost
d3 is shorter than d1
car is a stop word in this analyzer
explain: Same length and term frequency, so the difference is IDF: 1.992 for df 1 against 1.482 for df 2. Lucene's SynonymQuery avoids this by using the maximum df of the group.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Why the query the user typed is rarely the query to send
question: Which transformation is decomposition rather than rewriting or expansion?
options: Turning `how does it fail` into `how does Raft handle leader failure`
Appending `automobile` to a query that says `car`
Turning `compare Raft and Paxos leader election` into one query about Raft and one about Paxos
Correcting `recieve` to `receive`
explain: Decomposition produces several sub-queries that are retrieved separately. Resolving it to Raft and fixing a typo are rewrites (one query in, one query out); appending a synonym is expansion.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Interleave, step back, or fan out: IRCoT, Step-Back and multi-query
question: What is the key difference between IRCoT and Self-Ask?
options: IRCoT trains the retriever; Self-Ask does not
IRCoT uses each generated reasoning sentence as the next retrieval query, while Self-Ask writes explicit follow-up questions and inserts search answers
Self-Ask retrieves once; IRCoT retrieves once per document
They are the same algorithm with different names
explain: Both interleave retrieval with generation and both are prompting-only. Self-Ask sends explicit sub-questions to search and pastes back short answers; IRCoT sends its chain-of-thought sentences to a paragraph retriever and accumulates up to 15 paragraphs for a final reader.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: The unbiased estimator and its O(1/sqrt(D)) error
question: RaBitQ errors at D = 256 are too large for you. Following the 1/sqrt(D) rule, how many code bits per vector would halve the error?
explain: Error scales as 1/sqrt(D), so halving it needs 4x the bits: 1024. The paper notes you can lengthen codes by padding vectors with zeros before rotation; padded dimensions are not kept in the raw vectors.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Paxos: choosing one value with prepare and accept
question: A proposer finished phase 1 with number 7. Promises: A1 accepted (2, X), A2 accepted (4, Y), A3 accepted nothing. Which value must it send in accept(7, ?)
options: X, because it was accepted first
Its own value, because no value had a majority
Either X or Y, whichever it prefers
Y, the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal
explain: The rule picks the value of the highest-numbered proposal among the replies, here (4, Y). Y might already be chosen through a majority this proposer did not contact; (2, X) was never chosen: if it had been, every higher-numbered proposal issued, including (4, Y), would carry X.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Consensus in production: reads, membership, timeouts
question: With Pre-Vote enabled, a server returns after 10 minutes in a network partition. What happens to the current leader?
options: It steps down because the returning server has a much higher term
It must run a new election to admit the server
Nothing: the server never raised its term while isolated, and returns to follower when the leader's heartbeat reaches it
It is removed from the cluster configuration
explain: While partitioned, the server could not get pre-votes from a majority, so it never incremented its term. On reconnecting, the other servers are still hearing heartbeats and refuse its pre-vote; once the leader's heartbeat reaches it, it settles as a follower in the same term.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Prompting the generator to answer with citations
question: Which prompt change most directly reduces confident answers to questions the corpus cannot answer?
options: Raising the sampling temperature
Moving the question before the sources
Asking for longer answers
Instructing the model to say it does not know when the sources lack the answer
explain: Barnett et al.'s first failure point is a question the documents cannot answer, where the system should say it does not know but can be fooled into answering. An explicit abstain instruction is the first defense; checking it needs test questions whose answer is absent.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Query-document features: BM25 per field, coverage, proximity
question: Document X has the query terms in its body at positions 4, 5 and 6. Document Y has them at positions 2, 40 and 77. Their body BM25 scores are equal. Which feature tells them apart?
options: Body BM25 with a larger k1
Body coverage ratio
Body length
Minimum window (proximity)
explain: Both contain all terms, so coverage is 1.0 for both, and BM25 ignores positions entirely. Only a positional feature such as the minimum covering window (3 versus 76) separates them.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Feature logging: train on exactly the numbers you serve
question: Offline NDCG of the new model is excellent, but online it underperforms the old one. Features were computed by a Python script for training and by the search engine for serving. What is the first thing to check?
options: Whether the learning rate was too high
Whether NDCG is the right metric
Whether the model has too few trees
Whether the two pipelines produce identical feature values for the same query-document pairs
explain: Train/serve skew is the prime suspect when offline and online disagree. Log the engine's feature vectors for a sample of pairs and diff them against the script's values. Fixing the model cannot help if its inputs differ.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Implementation gotchas: ties, ideals, missing queries
question: A colleague's evaluation writes every result with score 0.0 and the correct rank in the rank column, then runs trec_eval. What happens?
options: All documents tie on score, so trec_eval orders them by docno string, scrambling the ranking
trec_eval uses the rank column, so results are correct
trec_eval rejects the file
trec_eval reports every metric as 0
explain: trec_eval sorts by the score column and breaks ties by docno (reverse string order); it never reads the rank column. With all scores equal, the ranking becomes an ordering of document IDs, and every rank-sensitive metric is measured on that order instead.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Queue pairs, work requests and the completion queue
question: Your QP is in RTR. Which is true?
options: It can process incoming messages but cannot yet post sends
It can post sends but not receive
It can do both; RTS only enables atomics
It cannot do anything until RTS
explain: RTR means ready to receive: receive processing starts at RTR. The transition to RTS adds the send-side parameters (send PSN, timeout, retry counts), after which ibv_post_send works.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: InfiniBand, RoCEv2 and iWARP: what carries the packets
question: In the victim-flow scenario, why is VS to VR slowed even though it never crosses the congested switch?
options: Because PFC pauses a whole port and priority, so every flow behind that port stops
Because ECN marks are broadcast to every flow
Because RoCE has no per-flow sequence numbers
Because DCQCN halves every flow's rate
explain: PFC is coarse: PAUSE frames apply per port and priority class. Cascading pauses reach ports that carry unrelated flows. Per-flow congestion control (DCQCN) keeps queues short so PAUSE is rarely needed.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Client-side prediction and server reconciliation
question: At t = 300 in the variant, the server reports x = 2 and last processed #3. Pending before filtering is [#3, #4]. What should the client do?
options: Keep showing 4 because its prediction is newer
Set x = 2, drop #3, replay #4 against the latest world
Set x = 2 and drop all pending inputs
Resend #3 and #4 to the server
explain: Inputs up to #3 are already reflected in x = 2, so #3 is dropped. #4 is still unconfirmed, so it is replayed on top of the authoritative state. Dropping #4 would lose a real input; resending would apply it twice.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Matrix factorization: learning user and item vectors
question: After one SGD update on the training pair (Ana, Space1), which parameters changed?
options: All user vectors, because the loss sums over everyone
Only Q[Space1]
Only P[Ana] and Q[Space1]
Every item vector Ana has rated
explain: The squared error for one rating depends only on p_u and q_i (plus their regularizers), so the stochastic gradient is zero for every other parameter. That is why SGD steps are cheap.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
question: Why not serve only the most popular items to every new user forever?
options: Popularity is a weak baseline that rarely beats random
Popularity cannot be computed in real time
It violates the cold-start assumption that new users have no context
It never collects feedback on other items or learns what each kind of user prefers; in our toy it earns 0.225 clicks per user vs 0.335 for LinUCB
explain: Popularity is a strong default (Hu et al. call it surprisingly powerful), but it is the same for everyone and is a feedback loop: unshown items stay unshown. A bandit trades a little short-term reward for information.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Three ways to join two tables
question: A query joins on `t1.hundred < t2.hundred` (an inequality). Which join algorithm can PostgreSQL use for this condition?
options: Hash join, because it is the fastest
Merge join, because both sides can be sorted
Nested loop, checking the condition for each pair
None; inequality joins are not supported
explain: Hash join needs equal keys to land in the same bucket, and PostgreSQL's merge join works on equality clauses of the form outerKey = innerKey.
